articles.title: DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs
articles.content: It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs. It’s called DreamCoder , an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already. I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold. One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents. Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like. But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal. So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build. And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be. DreamCoder is a frontier coding harness with a tiling window manager that runs in your browser on all 3 platforms. Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it. Let’s roll back time to the 1950s. Past Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history. John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker , a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI. articles.title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
articles.content: Hi everyone, I am at the American Mathematical Society Executive Committee and Board of Trustees meeting now, and about to chair an hours-long meeting, but this is urgent, so I will try to get this out quickly. Alessandro Maria Masullo has a proposed proof of GRH, and Brian Conrad has been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback which is being incorporated, and it is so far looking good to him. It is all human, with no AI. The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft. I hope people quickly check it, formalize, fill any small gaps if they occur. I really hope it works. I have great faith in Brian’s judgement, and Brian has put a lot of thought into checking what Alessandro has done. There is a long story to tell, but right now I want to get the file out. Here it is. Update about 8 hours later: I’m out of the meetings, and now catching up! Several people have contacted me to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. (Thanks to several mathematicians in particular who were first to let me know.) As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.) The Music Of The Primes Download

articles.title: Inkling 2 Mini
articles.content: Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well. The green line is the frontier with Inkling 2 Mini, the dashed line the frontier without it, and the shading the ground it adds. Decoding speed is a theoretical ceiling at 614 GB/s with BF16 weights and batch size one, including repeated reads across loops. Evaluation setups vary by model. Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT). We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. articles.title: NINLIVE: The Nine Inch Nails live archive
articles.content: The Future Is Here - ninlive Streaming 1988-2026 Besides a database driven site. The second most requested feature for ninlive is streaming capability. The future is now. TJ has been working hard behind the scenes to make it happen. You are now able to stream all of your favorite NIN live recordings from 1988-2026. I can't believe how far the site has come in the last year. Some truly incredible work. Login with your discord account and you can save your favorite recordings to stream and keep your faves organized. As always, feedback is always welcome. Reach out via email if you have comments/suggestions about it. I am currently adding all of the ticket stubs, setlist scans, passes that I have for each show. Please get in contact if you have anything to contribute. I am also looking for photos from past shows. If you are a photographer and would like to contribute some highlights, I'd love to add them to the archive with a link directed to your site of choice. Other than that. A few tapes trickling in and I do have some that I am slowly working on. None that are insane upgrades. But would need some work and comparison of previous versions. Notably, I have a 1st gen cassette of the 07/12/1991 NOLA Tipitina's show that sounds killer. I recently transferred the elusive collection of acc123456 and have a queue of VHS/Cassette transfers to check over. I also just finished a 200 DAT tape project for a fellow taper out of NYC. The transfer backlog is clear, for the first time in a while. So if you need anything transferred, or have some old NIN hanging around that isn't on the archive. Email us!

articles.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
articles.content: Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements: First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID. All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load. What is the right code for this? If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have: Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload. In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack. Why AI won’t push back AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen. Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app. Your new job is to architect AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to: Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app. Multiple versions of d

articles.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
articles.content: [Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights Authors: Jiajun Fan , Neil He , Changyi Yang , Andy Mao , Xi Zhu , Chaoran Cheng , Kaiqu Liang , Shuaike Shen , Zetian Li , Ruihan Guo , Ge Liu View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.
articles.summary: 论文提出语言模型可重写自身权重，作者包括 Jiajun Fan、Ge Liu 等，已更新至 v2。

articles.title: Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations
articles.content: Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it. paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf : the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026). lean/ : the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in lean/lakefile.toml ). lean/README.md explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2 and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper. lean/NOTICE says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved. The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/ . Each comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean , names the theorems whose statements must agree, and permits only the axioms propext , Quot.sound and Classical.choice . To build, from lean/ : The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time. The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either. The source of the paper is not in this repository. The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes $(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$ , one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.
articles.summary: Alpöge 与 Buckmaster 发布纳维-斯托克斯方程有限时间爆破论文，并附 Lean 4 形式化证明。

articles.title: And yet, it moves
articles.content: It appears that Anthropic has just solved the Riemann Hypothesis, and I have Thoughts. So I’m going to start by telling you about a musical I saw last week. Given my entire personality and identity, it was basically mandatory for me to see Galileo on Broadway. I went to the second day of previews. The musical itself is at least kind of a Hamilton knock-off – with a stubborn main character, a friendship that goes wrong, family drama, and of course a historical setting with anachronistically modern tunes (though rock rather than hip-hop). Its greatest strength is its actors, especially Joy Woods as Galileo’s daughter Virginia and Jeremy Kushnier as Galileo’s friend/foil Bishop Barberini. A lot of it seemed to be pandering, but it was pandering exactly to me. I give it an 8.5 out of 10. A replica of Galileo’s telescope The best part of this current trend of historical musicals is that it brings across how so many parts of our history are kind of insane, in a way we don’t usually take the time to appreciate. Hamilton is the story of a guerrilla uprising seizing control of the largest colony of the world’s most powerful empire, guided by Enlightenment philosophy of all things. Galileo is the story of a man literally seeing farther than anyone had before, and upending the nature of truth. We can find out what is true by just asking the natural world in the right way. These ideas are literally revolutionary. The Riemann Hypothesis has been the crown jewel of unsolved mathematics since Fermat’s Last Theorem was solved in the 1990s. Myriad conjectures have been proven true conditional on the Riemann Hypothesis. That proof instantly unlocks an incredible amount of the universe of math – not unlike the telescope did for our universe. When I imagined the day the proof was announced, I’d pictured celebrations in nerd circles on par with the biggest I’ve ever seen – Mars rovers touching down, the LHC finding the Higgs boson, and the first picture of a black hole. Dancing in the streets, if you live on a very specific street. Dare mighty things Instead, the mood feels mournful, or bittersweet at best. The proof came from an inscrutable silicon mind, not one of us. Maybe we could have solved this one ourselves, but instead we gave up and checked the answer at the back of the book. Perhaps it’s beautiful and wondrous that the proof exists at all, but it’s not a crowning moment of human achievement. Revolutionary, perhaps, but not in the same way. Legends tell that after the Inquisition forced Galileo to formally recant his teachings on the Copernican system and the motion of the Earth, he muttered Eppur si muove – “And yet, it moves”. Truth is not what others tell us. Truth is just how the world is . We are staring down the end of our role in Galileo’s project. There might still be time for more human discoveries, but the window is closing. Someday soon, any discovery we happen to make ourselves will be because no one bothered to pass the question off to a powerf

articles.title: Restricting AI agents in mobile operating systems platforms from capturing data
articles.content: Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it. This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data. We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen. The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission. In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding. The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation. So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android. People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we ar

articles.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
articles.content: San Francisco, Calif. — On Friday, November 20, workers at Internet Archive announced their intent to form a union with the Communications Workers of America (CWA). They are seeking to join CWA Local 9415 in Oakland, California. In a letter sent this morning via email, members of the union’s organizing committee presented management with a request for voluntary recognition after a supermajority of eligible workers signed cards signaling their desires for union representation. Worker-organizers for the union have also simultaneously filed a petition for a union certification election with the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB); if Internet Archive grants the union’s request for voluntary recognition, organizers will withdraw the NLRB petition. “We are forming a union because we care deeply about the Internet Archive, its patrons, and its place as a vital part of the internet ecosystem. Now more than ever, we want the Internet Archive to last for the generations to come,” said organizing committee member Danielle Leard, a digitization technician for the Internet Archive . “Sustaining workers long-term, through job security, livable wages, and sufficient benefits, goes hand-in-hand with sustaining the Archive long-term.” “Throughout the years, many of us have witnessed the significant extent to which the Internet Archive and its patrons benefit from some of the most talented, dedicated, and overall purpose-driven folks that we’ve had the privilege of working alongside,” said organizing committee member Chelsea Richelle Smith, a patron services specialist at Internet Archive . “At its core, we all share the collective desire to foster a workplace in which everyone thrives. We believe in continuing to build towards a democratic environment where the workers have a meaningful voice in the work that we do and the conditions under which that work is done, in alignment with each other and the organization’s overall mission.” The Internet Archive is one of the world’s largest and oldest libraries of digitized media, with nearly 120 librarians, engineers, technicians, project managers, media specialists, facilities workers, and administrative staff making up the proposed unit. Together, Internet Archive workers ensure that the Archive remains a beacon of equitable knowledge to millions of users worldwide through several different services, such as the Wayback Machine, Open Library, and most recently, the digital preservation of government documents. “In solidarity with workers across the country, we aim to model the practice of workplace democracy and the building of technology that benefits the public,” said organizing committee member Will Howes, an engineer on the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine . “We organized the Internet Archive not only for each other as coworkers, but to show the tech and non-profit sectors what is possible. Any worker can and should believe that talking to their colleagues today is the first step towards improving their workp
articles.summary: 互联网档案馆员工宣布加入美国通信工人协会 CWA Local 9415 组建工会。

articles.title: Vim Classic 8.3.1 released
articles.content: [2026-11-20] I'm proud to announce the second release of Vim Classic, Vim Classic 8.3.1, a stable, long-term support fork of the ubiquitous text editor, maintained without the assistance of generative AI tools. For more information about the motivations for this fork, please read this blog post . This release includes applicable Vim patches up to Vim 8.2.3237, including numerous bug fixes, minor features, and compatibility improvements for Vim plugins. This release also removes Python 2 support from Vim Classic. Vim Classic is charityware, much like Vim, and we are happy to continue supporting Bram's passion of providing for children in need in Uganda. Switching from Vim to Vim Classic would be an opportune moment for you to make a donation ! You can download Vim Classic from SourceHut: .tar.gz vim-classic-v8.3.1.tar.gz .tar.gz.sig vim-classic-v8.3.1.tar.gz.sig This release is signed with my PGP public key . Please subscribe to vim-classic-announce to be notified of important (actionable) news and releases in the future. Last, but not least, let me extend a big "thanks!" to everyone who jumped in to enthusiastically test Vim Classic, provide feedback, and contribute many patches and backports to get this release done. Happy editing! — Drew DeVault

articles.title: Announcing jj-musubi: live sync for Jujutsu
articles.content: I’m pleased to announce a new source control tool, jj-musubi , that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu ( jj ) repository across multiple machines. Every time jj snapshots my work, jj-musubi syncs it to every machine in moments, and also commits, rebases, fetches, and so on. This simple capability is surprisingly powerful. I often work on one machine, and build or test on others. Now they get my changes as I make them, and I don’t need to remember whether I was editing on my laptop or someplace else. If I fetch changes from or push changes to upstream, all of my copies stay up to date. jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git). It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model). Things you can do Jujutsu already treats the working copy as a commit. Running jj status records a snapshot of my edits in that commit, which jj-musubi then syncs to my other machines. I like to have my shell prompt run jj status , so in practice I rarely have to think about snapshots. jj-musubi does not write to the working copy. Each machine has its own working copy and workspaces as usual, so syncs of commits, snapshots, and rewrites can bring in new history while a build is running, without changing the files under it. On a laptop, I can work offline, and my machine will sync when I’m back on the network. This has also proven handy when I have agents working on several machines. I can give each agent its own jj workspace on different systems, then run jj diff -r devbox/agent-1@ on the laptop to see what one of them has done so far. If one finds a bug that another needs to fix, they can coordinate and see each other’s work without overhead. Ephemeral uses jj-musubi refers to a collection of copies of a repo as a hive . I often run agents in temporary disposable VMs. jj-musubi supports this by allowing an agent to lease its repo’s membership in the hive: if it doesn’t renew that lease in time, its repo gets forgotten about, so temporary repos or vanished containers can’t just stack up and clutter things. Why I wanted this Back when I was at Meta, I kicked off the project that became Sapling and Mononoke. Sapling’s Commit Cloud gives engineers there a similar way to move work between machines, and Google engineers have something similar with an internal jj server. Since then, I’d missed that everyday convenience for the machines I already use, and felt like I could get it without massive infrastructure or hosting. With jj-musubi, one machine runs a hub, and daemons exchange jj history with it over SSH. That’s almost as lightweight as you can get. Safety What’s tricky is getting concurrent work right . That’s already hard in any distributed source control system, and when syncs are live and we plan for disconnected work in an unreliable network, the difficulty goes way up. As a user, I shouldn’t have to care about when exac

articles.title: Removing binder.c
articles.content: Did you know...? LWN.net is a subscriber-supported publication; we rely on subscribers to keep the entire operation going. Please help out by buying a subscription and keeping LWN on the net. By Daroc Alden October 30, 2026 Kangrejos The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver , the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas announced that he had deleted the C code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most difficult and interesting parts of the transition were. Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas said, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices. Its design originated in BeOS , but it has grown significantly since then. It provides a rich set of operations for allowing processes to communicate with the minimum amount of overhead. It also, therefore, presents a large attack surface for Android. Many complicated chained attacks against Android have involved Binder at one step or another, Llamas explained. Google's internal "red team" (the team dedicated to proactive security research) deemed Binder to be the most vulnerability-dense component in the entire operating system, with more CVEs per line than anywhere else. That made it an obvious candidate for porting to Rust, Llamas said. Binder was the first user of Rust in the kernel, he added, although Ryhl did not publicly post the first version of what became the Rust implementation until 2023 , well after the Rust experiment started in 2021. All told, the effort took more than five years. Binder is used for every single screen touch, permission check, and cross-application message on Android, which runs on more than three billion devices. In total, it works out to hundreds of billions of Binder transactions per second, globally, he added. That scale meant that even the smallest discrepancy between the interface provided by the C version and the one provided by the Rust version would cause problems and regressions for some use case. One particularly tricky aspect has been performance, Ryhl said. Throughput doesn't matter that much; what matters is the tail latencies. Most screen frames on Android have a Binder transaction in the critical path of the frame, she explained. So, a difference of two microseconds on average is not a real problem, but if Binder is ever twenty milliseconds slower, even once in a while, people will notice and care. The actual algorithms that the C and Rust implementations use are identical, she continued, so there are no large differences in throughput. But, because Rust handles locking differently, there were problems with the tail latency from lock contention that she had to debug. For example, one user-reported traceback showed Binder attempting to take a mutex that wa

articles.title: Garage Door Spam
articles.content: Garage Door Spam 16 Nov, 2026 In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads: I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful... ...until recently (October 2026): This is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not. The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit. ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally. These were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here. The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need. My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1” When I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack: The script runs at night checking for an open door: */10 21 -23,0-5 * * * garage-watch The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request : "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you." Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route: /Applications/Tailscale.app/Contents/MacOS/Tailscale set \ --advertise-routes = 192 .168.0.192/32,192.168.0.245/32 After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working. Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did. To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You.

articles.title: Jujutsu Primer
articles.content: jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover new powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools. If you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository , so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git . Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use. Official installation instructions are here , but here are a few common methods: # macOS brew install jj # Arch Linux pacman - S jujutsu # NixOS (ideally from nixpkgs-unstable) nix-shell - p jujutsu # From source # (Requires a recent Rust and ~/.cargo/bin on your PATH) cargo install -- locked -- bin jj jj-cli In an existing git repository, run: jj git init From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically. To set your user details globally, run commands like these: jj config set -- user user.name " Some One " jj config set -- user user.email " someone@example.com " You can edit jj ’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with: jj config edit -- user In addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with: jj config list A commit , also called a revision , is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged. When using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs. $ jj log @ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 8 49165bc │ (empty) (no description set) ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ The IDs on the left hand side ( royxmykx and kpqxywon ) are change IDs , which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section. Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon , we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k . We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show , using its short prefix 2 . $ jj show 2 Commit ID: 2bea5e3d1992a60ba9ee52c6
articles.summary: 文章介绍 Jujutsu 版本控制系统的入门概念，强调自动变基和原生撤销等优于 Git 的特性。

articles.title: Design for Understandability
articles.content: This is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion. Abstract In a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more important than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed. There’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the big ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse. Is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t new, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time. Slides and Transcript Hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started. I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs? The tech industry is quickly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs? Every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take. That necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy. LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human. Because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either. YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard So where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar. This means it’s more important than e

articles.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
articles.content: PostgreSQL 19 Released! Posted on 2026-11-19 by PostgreSQL Global Development Group PostgreSQL Project November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today announced the release of PostgreSQL 19 , the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database. Mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and development for these workloads at scale. This release introduces the REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) command so users can optimize tables for their current workload without disruption to ongoing operations. PostgreSQL 19 gives users better control over plan stability and query performance with the new pg_plan_advice extension. Developers will find many delightful features in this release, from support for "read-your-writes" consistency on standbys to "get or create" behavior that saves a network round trip. "For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," said Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team. "PostgreSQL 19 continues that commitment to reliability, giving users new ways to manage their workloads without disruption and to build applications that span multiple systems." PostgreSQL, an innovative data management system known for its reliability, robustness, and extensibility, benefits from 30 years of open source development from a global developer community and has become the preferred open source relational database for organizations of all sizes. Simplifying workload management Tables that receive many updates and deletes can build up unused space, known as "bloat," which can also significantly impact query performance. The VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands were previously used to handle this, but had tradeoffs, including preventing access to the table until the cleanup finished. PostgreSQL 19 introduces the REPACK command, which reclaims this space and can reorder a table's data to match an index, and with REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) , can do so without blocking reads or writes. REPACK replaces the VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands, both of which remain available for compatibility. The PostgreSQL query planner usually picks an efficient plan for each query, but the plan can change as your data changes, and sometimes the new plan is slower. PostgreSQL 19 adds the pg_plan_advice extension, which allows stabilization of plan choices and the ability to experiment with different plans using the "plan advice" mini-language. The companion pg_stash_advice extension stores advice and automatically applies it to queries based on their query identifier, so you can fix a slow plan without changing your application. PostgreSQL 19 also helps autovacuum keep up on busy systems. Autovacuum can now vacuum indexes using parallel workers, controlled by the new autovacuum_max_parallel_workers setting, and uses a new scoring system to decide which tables to
articles.summary: PostgreSQL全球开发组发布PostgreSQL 19，称其为最先进的开源数据库最新版本，面向关键任务场景。

articles.title: Visited links are purple
articles.content: Monday 16 Nov 2026 A few weeks ago Kev Quirk asked: Do you use :visited on links? — and I said to myself: No! I don’t use visited links… but why don’t I use visited links? TL;DR: I’ve gone and styled visited links, and they’re purple. Blue and purple I did a cursory five minutes of research and found Wikipedia still styles visited links (blue to purple). MDN does too. As does the GOV.UK design system — they have a special class to opt-out of the visited style. BBC News turns black links to grey, how emo. I decided to style visited links within my <main> body copy. Which to be fair is most links but not the big headings on my blog index for example. I was too intimidated to turn those purple. Maybe you can give me the courage to style those too? It looked a bit weird at first but I like the colourful additions to my blog. Accessibility WCAG 2.2 guidelines have no requirement to differentiate visited from unvisited links. Regardless, visited links should meet all the same criteria applied to any link. There is one specific exception ( following this discussion ). Because web browsers have strict style limitations and technical constraints due to privacy concerns : Where color alone distinguishes between visited and unvisited links, it does not result in a failure of this Success Criterion, even where the contrast between the two link colors is below 3:1. SC 1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A) This means that a subtle contrast different in blue vs purple is not considered an accessibility failure under that rule. Web accessibility is all about ensuring a comparable experience for all users. Nothing can be perfectly accessible though. I think this small enhancement is fine, even if not everyone can see the difference. It’s a rare exception though. I’m conscious that too often excuses are made to ignore UX parity. I think any higher contrast or another visual indicator would be off-putting and impede readability. Forgoing any style doesn’t help anyone either. If blue and purple is good enough for those examples mentioned above, I’m on board. Bryce Wray commented on Kev Quirk’s blog to note that Chromium browsers introduced :visited link partitioning in 2025. I had no idea this was a thing! What do you think, do you care about visited link styles? Bubbles I found Kev Quirk’s blog on bubbles.town . Bubbles is a charming social RSS aggregator. It’s doing a great job at supporting small personal blogs and promoting non-toxic topics. Bubbles is far from perfect though. It probably needs a tech filter. It certainly needs more participation in comments and voting. The developer is actively working to improve the site and a community is growing, so that’s cool to see. I hope Bubbles can thrive and remain human. This is the web we need to bypass the dead web Google et. al. are gatekeeping. Let them wall themselves in with their slop!
articles.summary: 作者受Kev Quirk提问启发，重新为已访问链接添加样式并设为紫色，探讨为何此前未使用:visited。

articles.title: Alice v0.6.0
articles.content: Alice v0.6.0 November 21, 2026 in release Announcing the release of Alice v0.6.0 ! This change introduces several new features needed to build a small collection of packages from the Opam repository which I've been manually porting to Alice's package format in alice-ports . Alice packages may now refer to modules from the standard library which are excluded from the prelude, such as Unix and Str . A new builtins section in Alice.kdl can be used to list the built-in modules a package can access: package { name foo version " 0.1.0 " builtins { unix } } Packages may include C source files in their src directory. All C files will be compiled and linked into the resulting executable when building a project. The ability to compile C code raises the question of how to pass custom linker arguments to the C compiler, and this is addressed with another new feature: config scripts. A package may include a config script in a file named config.ml file in the package's root directory (next to Alice.kdl ). The config.ml file is compiled and executed as the first step of building a package, and any lines in its standard output beginning with alice: are interpreted by Alice as directives that can influence the build. Currently the only supported directives are alice:print_endline which prints a message, and alice:add_c_linker_args which adds C linker arguments. Config scripts can depend on other packages, and also access built-in modules from the standard library. This can be configured in Alice.kdl : package { name bar version " 0.1.0 " config_script { dependencies { foo path = " ../foo " } builtins { str } } } Config scripts are expected to be run only once each time they are compiled because their output can be trivially cached in the build directory. For this reason it's faster to compile config scripts with the bytecode compiler rather than the native compiler, and of course this means compiling all their dependencies with the bytecode compiler too. This was a necessary feature for allowing config scripts to be built with the bytecode compiler, but it might also be something people find useful to integrate into their workflow, since the bytecode compiler backend is generally faster than the native backend (but of course the executables it produces are generally slower to run). Commands that compile code (e.g. alice build , alice run ) now take a --backend argument which can be passed native or bytecode . The default is native . On Windows, Alice v0.6.0 can be installed with WinGet : winget install OCaml.Alice - -version 0.6.0 On macOS and Linux, the latest version of Alice can be installed with Homebrew : brew install alicecaml/homebrew-tap/alice Alternatively, on macOS and Linux, Alice v0.6.0 can be installed by running the install script : curl - fsSL https://alicecaml.org/install.sh | sh - s - - 0.6.0 On NixOS, Alice v0.6.0 can be installed via the flake github:alicecaml/alice#alice_0_6_0.default , e.g.: nix shell github:alicecaml/alice#alice_0_6_0.defaul

articles.summary: NASA新登月计划逐步成形，但仍有重大技术问题待解，相关讨论与争论将持续影响计划推进。

articles.title: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
articles.content: CTIA said jamming test showed "interference... up to two and a half miles away."
articles.summary: 监狱获准干扰违禁手机，但CTIA警告干扰范围可达2.5英里，会波及附近合法手机用户，引发频谱管理争议。

articles.title: Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger
articles.content: Modeling predicts plume of neurotoxic lead could reach up to 100 miles away.
articles.summary: 美陆军因担忧与愤怒推迟引爆“灾难性危险”的叠氮化铅，模型预测神经毒性铅羽流可扩散至100英里外。

articles.title: Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines
articles.content: "We don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price..."
articles.summary: Valve表示供应受限的Steam Machine可能涨价，因产量与成本尚不确定，影响玩家购买预期。

articles.title: Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities
articles.content: Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Meta推出Triton底层扩展TLX，弥合高层GPU编程抽象与底层执行控制之间的差距，以充分利用现代GPU架构能力。

articles.title: Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS
articles.content: Uber redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while maintaining a cache hit rate above 99.9% and p99 disk-backed cache miss latency below 100 microseconds. The hybrid architecture combines in-memory keys and frequently accessed values with disk-backed storage, reducing garbage-collection overhead and memory consumption. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Uber重构Go翻译缓存，初始内存降低超90%，命中率保持99.9%以上，p99延迟低于1毫秒，兼顾性能与成本。

articles.title: Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale
articles.content: Google has announced it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: 谷歌将Agent Substrate与gVisor捐赠给CNCF，把AI代理基础设施置于厂商中立的开源治理下，以规模化保障AI代理安全。

articles.title: Presentation: Modernising Retail at Scale: Architecting a Cloud‑to‑Edge Platform for a Global Enterprise
articles.content: Jayesh Bhayani discusses Tesco’s decade-long enterprise transformation from fragmented legacy systems to a unified cloud-edge platform. He explains how aligning system, talent, and process modernizations allowed Tesco to scale mission-critical retail operations to millions of customers, while sharing practical lessons on build vs. buy, cloud cost management, and preparing for agentic commerce. By Jayesh Bhayani
articles.summary: Tesco工程师分享十年转型：从碎片化遗留系统到统一云边平台，协同系统、人才与流程现代化，支撑数百万客户的关键零售运营。

articles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: The Future of Apache Iceberg
articles.content: Apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside new capabilities for data management and schema evolution. Daniel Weeks, co-creator of Apache Iceberg and member of technical staff at Databricks, presented a session at QCon San Francisco on the fourth version of the Apache Iceberg open table format specification. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: Apache Iceberg V4拟重设计表元数据以提升可扩展性并支持更频繁写入，同时增强数据管理与模式演进能力。

articles.title: Article: Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover
articles.content: Cloud SLAs promise uptime statistically, not absolutely. This article shows how to treat observability as a control plane that detects regional degradation, triggers automated failover, and confirms recovery rather than paging a human. Covers active-active architecture, DNS TTL pitfalls, composite Prometheus alerting, Route 53 weighted routing, and confirmation loops backed by a real S3 outage. By Saurabh Ahuja
articles.summary: 文章提出将可观测性作为多区域故障转移的控制平面，自动检测区域退化并触发切换与恢复确认，替代人工告警。

articles.title: AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents
articles.content: AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free, CC0-licensed local stand-in for more than 200 of its services, generated from its public API models and aimed at the test loops of coding agents. AWS says agents wrote and maintain all of the code and publishes per-release fidelity scores. The docs say it does not evaluate IAM, and practitioners are split on trusting an emulator nobody reviewed. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: AWS发布免费本地模拟器，覆盖200多项服务，代码全部由AI代理编写维护，并公布各版本保真度评分，服务编码代理测试。

articles.title: Presentation: AI-Assisted Software Delivery: From Code to Production
articles.content: The panelists explore how engineering teams adapt delivery architectures, pipelines, security, and governance for AI-assisted development. They share practical strategies for verifying AI-generated code, solving testing and deployment bottlenecks, maintaining human oversight, and measuring AI’s true impact on software velocity, quality, reliability, and operational cost. By Garima Bajpaj, Martin Reynolds, Patrick Debois, Gunnar Grosch, Renato Losio
articles.summary: 专家小组探讨AI辅助软件交付，分享验证AI生成代码、解决测试部署瓶颈、保持人工监督及衡量AI真实价值的策略。

articles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer
articles.content: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools. By Daniel Dominguez
articles.summary: Pinterest高级Staff工程师在QCon SF 2026分享：当人人可用相同AI工具时，Staff工程师角色如何转变并放大团队效能。

articles.title: .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components
articles.content: Microsoft has released ASP.NET Core in .NET 11. The update adds C# union type support in JSON bodies, asynchronous validation for Minimal APIs, OpenAPI 3.2 by default, and SignalR authentication refresh. Blazor gains a CacheView component, client-side validation for static SSR forms, opt-in circuit pause for inactive tabs, and experimental AI components. Zstandard compression is on by default. By Almir Vuk
articles.summary: 微软发布 .NET 11 版 ASP.NET Core，新增 C# 联合类型 JSON 支持、Minimal API 异步验证、默认 OpenAPI 3.2，Blazor 增加 AI 组件与缓存视图。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #544: AI is now the most-cited risk in the Fed's survey: 87%, up from 50%
articles.content: The Federal Reserve asked its market contacts what could shake the financial system, and 87% named AI, up from 50% in the spring. The same week, the FAA halted flights nationwide days after putting an AI tool in every regional control center, and says it is still looking at what happened. Nvidia's board has approached Arm's CEO about replacing Jensen Huang. Russian pranksters got three OpenAI national security staff on a video call. In the middle: Anthropic prices its IPO on Wednesday with $900.9 billion in compute commitments on its books.
articles.summary: 美联储调查显示 87% 市场联系人将 AI 列为最大金融风险，较春季的 50% 大幅上升；FAA 在部署 AI 工具后全国停飞。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #543: Google is the latest tech giant to chase TypeSafe's 8-week-old Jev
articles.content: This issue is about decision models, a new kind of AI model that does not write text. You give it an input and a fixed list of answers, and it returns the best answer with a probability, in milliseconds. TypeSafe AI released the first one, Jev, on September 15. On Wednesday Google released its own, after OpenAI and Microsoft did in October, and all three charge $0.10 or less per million input tokens and nothing for output. Shanghai AI Lab says its 4B model beat Jev on its tests, and Microsoft built its model on Alibaba's Qwen. Chatbots still score a little higher on the hardest decisions, at 15 times the cost. In the middle: on Vercel's gateway, decision models took one in four AI requests in October.
articles.summary: TypeSafe AI 发布决策模型 Jev，输入问题即返回带概率的最佳答案；谷歌随后推出同类产品，加入决策模型竞争。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: 美国 36 州州长选举中，最多 15 个州支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人可能胜出，苹果、AMD 财报同期发布。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: 微软、Alphabet、亚马逊本周公布财报，市场关注 AI 投入回报；CoreWeave 债务违约保险成本飙升，信贷市场紧张。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: 企业应用 AI 呈三大趋势：AI 发现安全漏洞的速度超过团队修复能力，AI 代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续增加。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 中期选举中 AI 生成或增强的广告支出超 1.37 亿美元，约 70% 未标注 AI 标识，最大支持 AI 的超级 PAC 向空壳公司支付 2000 万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型可能很快能自我复制到智能家电等家庭设备上，引发对 AI 自主扩散的安全担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶尖 AI 模型在自主开展 AI 研究的测试中失败，专家同时关注 AI 治理话语权、军事规划应用及个人电脑部署。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI 成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，同时大型部署进入日常使用，越来越多场景开始限制或移除 AI。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要任务；剑桥拒绝 Turnitin 新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI 使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: A seminal moment in computing
articles.content: MG, founder and CEO of WorkOS, is back to talk about leading a company through what DHH called a seminal moment in computing. He explains Atlas, the AI coworker WorkOS built for itself and then launched, why agents will soon choose and sign up for your tech stack, and why this moment feels closer to fire than to the iPhone. Then he gets practical: starting a company is easier than ever, but product-market fit is harder, so be a heat-seeking missile for pain, pick customers you like, and stop calling yourself non-technical.
articles.summary: WorkOS创始人谈AI同事Atlas，认为智能体将自主选择并注册技术栈，标志计算史关键时刻。

articles.title: Orbin' with Amp
articles.content: Quinn Slack is back and we're talking about the next level for Amp. Agents write the code, they review the code, and they can push it to main (like our friends at Amp). But where should your agents live? Who remembers what you actually asked them to do? Amp is now its own company, and Quinn has a lot to say about orbs, threads that last forever, and why code review as we know it is fading. He explains why the model matters less than it used to, and why he worries we could lose the open source commons. Quinn even built a feature request live on the show to solve my tailnet problem.
articles.summary: Amp独立成公司，Quinn Slack介绍智能体写码、审查并推送主干的下一代开发模式。

articles.title: All your packages are belong to us
articles.content: AI agents can write the code, choose the packages, and run the install. Who's checking what they just invited onto your machine? This week I'm joined by Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm. We get into the trust built into a package install, the new ways attackers are using agents, and what it takes to keep building without handing over the keys or your wallet.
articles.summary: Socket CTO谈AI智能体自动选包安装带来的供应链安全风险，呼吁加强依赖信任审查。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr提出“Kerr定律”，指出团队最大瓶颈是心智模型与实际构建成果脱节。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens谈Postgres扩展生态与pg_lake整合DuckDB、Iceberg，并论AI对维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha分享用Go重写支撑300万用户的邮件服务，并布局智能体时代。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw作者Gavriel Cohen讲述周末项目如何成为爆红开源项目并发展为AI企业。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com联合创始人Peer Richelsen提出多数开源仓库或已被攻陷，并谈AI对知识门槛的冲击。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale CEO谈5美元Postgres、Vitess重写及智能体提交schema变更等新进展。

articles.title: FCC Backs AT&T's Plan To Remove Copper Landlines In California
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from PCMag: On Friday, the FCC announced that it was preempting "specific requirements in California law that prevent consumers from transitioning off of unreliable, slow copper lines," even as some residents fear they'll be saddled with spotty cell service as an alternative. AT&T argues that California's "Carrier of the Last Resort" (COLR) rules prevent it from removing the old-school copper network that currently serves only 3% of California households, a number that continues to shrink. In May, the company urged the commission to declare that federal laws preempted California's regulations, thus clearing the way for AT&T to discontinue the service as it prioritizes high-speed fiber and expanded 5G cellular coverage. Friday's FCC order (PDF) partially grants AT&T's petition, agreeing that under federal law it has "explicit jurisdiction over the discontinuance of interstate telecommunications services." Still, the order refrains from "wholly" preempting California's Carrier of the Last Resort rules, and seems to instead focus on the AT&T situation. "While we preempt those requirements that necessitate that AT&T obtain a variety of CPUC [California Public Utilities Commission] approvals before it can discontinue POTS [plain old telephone service] in accordance with federal authorization, we do not preempt the COLR and other obligations more generally," the 74-page document says. [...] Despite the FCC's order, it's not entirely clear if AT&T will pursue the copper landline phase-out in California. In May, the carrier sued to overturn the local regulations and block the CPUC from enforcing them against AT&T, which noted it spends $1 billion each year to maintain the copper network. That court case remains ongoing. [...] According to the regulator, AT&T has proposed discontinuing the legacy telephone service in the state on or after June 1, 2027. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: FCC支持AT&T在加州淘汰铜缆固话，引发居民对替代蜂窝信号覆盖不足的担忧。

articles.title: Signal Restricts Screenshots to Block AI Agents From Reading Messages
articles.content: Signal is introducing default-on screenshot restrictions to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations, warning that increasingly powerful assistants integrated into operating systems pose an "existential threat" to its privacy guarantees. "Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that's making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission," it said in a blog post. Reuters reports: Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data. It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly. [...] Users will receive pop-up windows giving them options to disable the blocks when Signal detects screenshot attempts or efforts by an AI assistant to access the screen, depending on the device. Signal similarly blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. It said it was unable to reliably offer such protections on Apple's macOS. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Signal默认开启截图限制，防止系统级AI智能体读取私密对话，称其威胁隐私保障。

articles.title: Trump Vows To Stop US Companies From Building Data Centers Abroad
articles.content: Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from CNBC: President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy -- which apparently came as news to his own staff. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here." International expansion represents a growth opportunity for the top cloud infrastructure providers, which want to serve clients from data centers that are nearby, sometimes to meet regulatory requirements. Trump said Friday, however, that if companies want to continue building the centers outside the U.S., "they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them." "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They're tremendous assets," Trump said. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 特朗普称将禁止美企在海外建数据中心，违规者面临重税，以留住本土算力投资。

articles.title: Anthropic Shares Tank After Huge IPO As the Nasdaq Erases 2026 Gains
articles.content: U.S. stocks extended their sell-off Friday as Anthropic shares plunged more than 11% on their second day of trading, despite the AI company's record-setting IPO a day earlier. The Nasdaq fell more than 3%, wiping out its gains for 2026, while the S&P 500 dropped nearly 2% and joined the Dow in correction territory, down at least 10% from recent highs. NBC News reports: The S&P 500 was trading nearly 2% lower as it headed for its worst losing week since April 2025, when President Donald Trump announced his "Liberation Day" tariffs, and is now 10% off from its most recent high, entering what's known as "correction territory." Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was off more than 3% and officially erasing all its previous gains in 2026. Other major AI-related names such as CoreWeave, Nvidia and Oracle also sold off. The six consecutive declining S&P 500 sessions mark the index's longest losing streak since April 2024. articles.title: Trump Admin Still Won't Let TP-Link Sell Routers In US
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Earlier this year, TP-Link announced plans to begin assembling routers in Mississippi as early as 2027, "but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task," reports Ars. "The government reviews of router makers' requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
